I think that, at least in the United States, voting doesn't make a difference because in the end it's not the elected officials that really run the country. You may think Democrats and Republicans are different because: gay marriage, abortion, etc. But the candidates that eventually get to run against each other are the same in everything that would actually make a difference. They are both for getting as much money as they can from the rich ruling class, and then giving the rich ruling class all they want in the hope that they themselves are allowed to become, or stay, part of the rich ruling class. Everything else we see is just political theater to appease the masses.

Everybody saying voting matters (and implying that it matters on a national level in the United States) has yet to even cursorily address three things:

  • The Electoral College
  • Gerrymandering and the consequent running unopposed for many, many offices.
  • The phenomenon of having your guy win, only to be corrupted in short order by perverse and pervasive incentives. (Lobbyists and a defunct press.)

There's actually a lot of research that indicates that not only does an individual vote not matter, popular opinion no longer matters in the American system. Even if you could successfully motivate an entire demographic to vote, it's highly unlikely that effective policy change would ensue. I'm with OP. Things will have to degenerate to a crisis that unmakes and remakes the social order--a revolution isn't necessary, but we are talking about sweeping changes on the order of the New Deal. The only things that precipitate such changes are things like the Great Depression and WWII.

Maybe, maybe if Sarbanes and Durbin's bill that gives citizens tax credits for political contributions passes, then maybe the current system will have enough citizen influence on it to begin to reflect popular opinion, but even then, we're not talking about voting making a difference.
